title: The River Bank
paragraphs: The Mole had been working hard all morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First he used brooms, then dusters; then he climbed up ladders and steps and chairs with a brush and a bucket of whitewash, until his throat and eyes were full of dust, his black fur was spattered with whitewash, and his back ached and his arms were tired out. Spring was stirring in the air above him and in the earth below and all around, and it crept even into his dark, humble little house, bringing a restless, almost holy longing for something more. So it was hardly surprising that he suddenly threw his brush on the floor, said “Bother!” and “Oh, blow!” and then “To blazes with spring-cleaning!” and dashed out of the house without even stopping to grab his coat. Something above was calling him, and he would not be refused. He headed for the steep little tunnel that served him as the gravel driveway owned by animals whose homes are closer to the sun and air. So he scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged, and then he scrooged again and scrabbled and scratched and scraped, working busily with his little paws and muttering to himself, “Up we go! Up we go!” until at last, pop! his snout came out into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

“This is wonderful!” he told himself. “This is much better than whitewashing!” The sun beat warm on his fur, soft breezes stroked his hot forehead, and after so long shut away in his cellar-like home, the songs of happy birds sounded almost like shouting to his dulled ears. He bounded along with all four legs off the ground at once, thrilled to be alive and to enjoy spring without any of its cleaning, and made his way across the meadow until he reached the hedge on the far side.

“Halt!” said an elderly rabbit at a gap in the hedge. “Sixpence to use this private road!” In an instant the impatient, scornful Mole had knocked him head over heels and trotted on along the hedge, teasing the other rabbits as they peeked out of their holes in a hurry to see what the commotion was. “Onion sauce! Onion sauce!” he called mockingly, and he was gone before they could think of a really satisfying reply. Then they all began to squabble with one another. “How _stupid_ you are! Why didn’t you tell him——” “Well, why didn’t _you_ say——” “You could have reminded him——” and so on, as usual; but of course by then it was far too late, as it always is.

It all seemed too good to be true. He wandered busily this way and that through the meadows, along the hedgerows and across the thickets, and everywhere he found birds building nests, flowers budding, and leaves pushing out—everything cheerful and active and hard at work. And instead of a guilty conscience nagging at him and whispering “whitewash!” he somehow could only feel how delightful it was to be the one lazy dog among all these busy citizens. After all, the best part of a holiday is perhaps not so much resting yourself as watching everyone else hard at work.

He thought his happiness could not be greater when, wandering along without any aim, he suddenly found himself standing at the edge of a brimming river. He had never seen a river before in his life. It was a sleek, winding, full-bodied creature, chasing and chuckling, grabbing things with a gurgle and letting them go with a laugh. Then it would fling itself on new playmates who shook themselves free and were caught and held again. Everything quivered and shimmered—glints and gleams and sparkles, rustle and swirl, chatter and bubble. The Mole was bewitched, entranced, fascinated. He trotted beside the river the way a very small child trots beside a man who holds him spellbound with exciting stories. When he was tired at last, he sat down on the bank while the river kept chattering to him. It was a babbling parade of the best stories in the world, sent from the heart of the earth to be told at last to the hungry sea.

As he sat on the grass looking across the river, a dark hole in the opposite bank, just above the water’s edge, caught his eye. He began dreamily to think what a cozy home it would make for an animal with few needs who liked a small, stylish riverside house, above the flood line and far from noise and dust. As he gazed, something bright and small seemed to twinkle in the depths of it, vanished, then twinkled again like a tiny star. But it could hardly be a star in such an unlikely place, and it was too bright and too small for a glow-worm. Then, as he watched, it winked at him, and so showed itself to be an eye; and a small face slowly began to form around it, like a frame around a picture.
A small brown face, with whiskers.
The face was round and solemn, and in its eyes was the very same twinkle that had drawn his attention at the start.
Small neat ears and thick silky fur.
It was the Water Rat!
Then the two animals stood there and eyed each other warily.
“Hello, Mole!” said the Water Rat.
“Hello, Rat!” said the Mole.
“Would you like to come across?” asked the Rat after a moment.
“Oh, it’s all very well to _talk_,” said the Mole, rather crossly, since he was new to rivers and riverside life and how things worked there.

The Rat said nothing, but bent down, untied a rope and pulled on it; then he stepped lightly into a little boat that the Mole had not noticed. It was painted blue on the outside and white on the inside, and it was just big enough for two animals; and the Mole’s whole heart went out to it at once, even though he did not yet fully understand what it was for.

The Rat rowed quickly across and tied up. Then he held out his forepaw as the Mole stepped carefully down. “Lean on that!” he said. “Now then, step lively!” and to his surprise and delight the Mole found himself actually sitting in the back of a real boat.
“What a wonderful day this has been!” he said, while the Rat pushed away from the bank and took up the oars once more. “Do you know, in my whole life I’ve never set foot in a boat before.”
“What?” cried the Rat, his jaw dropping. “Never set foot in a—you never—well, I—so what on earth have you been doing all this time?”

“Is it really that nice?” asked the Mole shyly, though he was quite ready to believe it as he leaned back in his seat and looked over the cushions, the oars, the oarlocks and all the fascinating fittings, and felt the boat rock gently beneath him.

“Nice? It’s the _only_ thing,” the Water Rat said gravely, leaning forward for his stroke. “Believe me, young friend, there is _nothing_—absolutely nothing—that’s half as worthwhile as simply messing about in boats. Just messing,” he went on in a dream: “messing—about—in—boats; messing——”
“Watch out, Rat!” the Mole cried suddenly.
Too late. The boat plowed straight into the bank, and the dreamer, the delighted oarsman, tumbled over backwards and ended up flat in the bottom of the boat with his feet sticking up in the air.

“—about in boats—or _with_ boats,” the Rat went on, quite unruffled, as he got to his feet with a good-natured laugh. “Whether you’re in them or out of them hardly matters. Nothing much matters at all, and that’s what is so delightful. You can get away or not get away; you can arrive where you were headed, or turn up somewhere else entirely, or go nowhere whatsoever, and either way you’re always busy and never doing anything in particular. Once you’ve finished, there’s always something else waiting, which you may do if you feel like it, though you’d be far better off leaving it alone. Listen! If you really have nothing else planned for this morning, why don’t we float off down the river together and spend a whole long day at it?”

Mole wriggled his toes for sheer joy, let out a deep sigh of perfect contentment that swelled his chest, and sank back blissfully into the soft cushions. “I’m having the most _marvelous_ day!” he said. “Come on, let’s get going right away!”

“Wait just a moment, then!” said the Rat. He slipped the rope through a ring on his landing-stage and scrambled up to his hole above. After a little while he came back into view, staggering beneath a plump wicker picnic basket.
“Stow that down by your feet,” he told Mole as he lowered it into the boat. Then he cast off the rope and picked up the oars again.
“What’s in it?” asked the Mole, wriggling with curiosity.
“There’s cold chicken in it,” replied the Rat shortly; “ coldtonguecoldhamcoldbeefpickledgherkinssaladfrenchrollscresssandwiches pottedme atgingerbeerlemonadesodawater——”
“Oh, stop, stop,” cried the Mole in ecstasy. “This is too much!”

“Do you honestly think so?” asked the Rat, in all seriousness. “It’s only what I always bring along on little outings like this. The other animals keep telling me I’m stingy, and that I _barely_ pack enough!”

The Mole never heard a word he said. Absorbed in the new life he was entering, drunk on the sparkle, the ripple, the scents and sounds and sunlight, he trailed a paw in the water and dreamed long daydreams. The Water Rat, good little fellow that he was, rowed steadily on and kindly left him alone.
“I do like your clothes, old chap,” he said, after some thirty minutes had gone by. “One of these days I mean to buy myself a black velvet smoking jacket, the moment I can afford one.”
“Oh, forgive me,” said the Mole, shaking himself awake with an effort. “You must think I’m dreadfully rude; it’s just that all of this is so new to me. And so—this—is—a—River!”
“_The_ River,” the Rat corrected him.
“And you really live by the river? What a lovely life!”

“By it, and with it, and on it, and in it,” said the Rat. “It’s my brother and my sister, my aunts, my company, my food and drink, and (naturally) my laundry. It’s my whole world, and I want no other. Whatever it lacks isn’t worth having, and whatever it doesn’t know isn’t worth knowing. Goodness, the times we’ve had together! Winter or summer, spring or autumn, it always has some fun and excitement to offer. In February, when the floods come up, my cellars and basement fill to the brim with drink I can’t use, and the brown water slides past my best bedroom window. Or else when it all drains away and leaves patches of mud that smell like plum-cake, with rushes and weeds choking the channels, and I can potter around with dry feet over most of the riverbed, finding fresh things to eat and all the odds and ends that careless people have let fall out of their boats!”
“But doesn’t it get dull sometimes?” the Mole dared to ask. “Only you and the river all day, with nobody else to chat with?”

“Nobody else to—well, I shouldn’t be hard on you,” said the Rat, holding back his temper. “You’re new here, and naturally you wouldn’t know. These days the riverbank is so crowded that plenty of folk are leaving altogether: oh no, it’s nothing like it used to be. Otters, kingfishers, dabchicks, moorhens, all of them underfoot from morning to night and forever wanting you to _do_ something—as though a fellow had no affairs of his own to look after!”
“What’s over _there?_” asked the Mole, waving a paw toward a backdrop of woodland that framed the water meadows darkly on one side of the river.
“That? Oh, that’s only the Wild Wood,” the Rat answered curtly. “We river-bankers don’t go in there much.”
“Aren’t they—aren’t they very _nice_ people in there?” asked the Mole, a little nervously.

“W-e-ll,” said the Rat, “let me think. The squirrels are fine. _And_ the rabbits—a few of them, though rabbits are a mixed bunch. And then of course there’s Badger. He lives right in the middle of it, and he wouldn’t live anywhere else, not for any money. Dear old Badger! Nobody meddles with _him_. They know better,” he added, with a look.
“Why, who _would_ interfere with him?” asked the Mole.
“Well, of course—there—are others,” the Rat explained, hesitating.

“Weasels—and stoats—and foxes—and the like. They’re decent enough in their way—I get on very well with them—we greet each other when we meet, and so on—but now and then they turn wild, there’s no getting around it, and then—well, you simply can’t trust them, and that’s the truth.”
The Mole knew very well that animal manners forbid dwelling on possible trouble ahead, or even hinting at it; so he dropped the subject.
“And beyond the Wild Wood?” he asked. “Where everything is blue and hazy, and you can see what might be hills or might not, and something like the smoke of towns, or is it only drifting cloud?”

“Beyond the Wild Wood comes the Wide World,” said the Rat. “And that’s something that doesn’t matter to either of us. I’ve never been there, and I’m never going, and neither are you, if you have any sense at all. Please don’t ever mention it again. Now then! Here at last is our backwater, where we’re going to have lunch.”

Leaving the main stream, they now glided into what looked at first like a little lake with land all around it. Green turf sloped down to either edge, and brown, snaky tree roots gleamed beneath the surface of the quiet water. Ahead of them the silvery shoulder and foamy tumble of a weir, arm in arm with a restless, dripping mill-wheel that in turn held up a gray-gabled mill house, filled the air with a soothing murmur, dull and muffled, yet with little clear voices speaking up cheerfully out of it now and then. It was so beautiful that the Mole could only hold up both forepaws and gasp, “Oh my! Oh my! Oh my!”

The Rat steered the boat in to the bank, tied her up, helped Mole, who was still unsteady on his feet, safely onto land, and swung out the lunch hamper. Mole begged, as a special favor, to be allowed to unpack everything on his own, and the Rat was delighted to humor him and stretch out full-length on the grass for a rest. Meanwhile his excited friend shook out the tablecloth and spread it, took the mysterious parcels out one at a time and laid out what was inside them in proper order, gasping “Oh my! Oh my!” at every new surprise. When everything was ready, the Rat said, “Now, dig in, old fellow!” And Mole was only too glad to obey. He had begun his spring-cleaning very early that morning, as people _will_ do, and hadn’t stopped for a bite or a sip since, and a great deal had happened to him since that faraway moment, which now felt like days ago.
“What are you looking at?” said the Rat after a while, when the edge of their hunger had been dulled and the Mole’s eyes could wander off the tablecloth a little.
“What I’m watching,” said Mole, “is a line of bubbles that I can see moving along the top of the water. It strikes me as rather funny.”
“Bubbles? Aha!” said the Rat, and he chirped cheerfully in an inviting sort of way.
A broad, shiny snout poked up over the lip of the bank, and then the Otter heaved himself out of the river and shook the water off his fur.
“Greedy rascals!” he said, heading for the food. “Why didn’t you invite me, Ratty?”
“This was a last-minute affair,” the Rat explained. “By the way—my friend Mr. Mole.”
“Pleased to meet you, I’m sure,” said the Otter, and the two animals were friends at once.

“Such a racket everywhere!” the Otter went on. “All the world seems to be out on the river today. I came up this backwater to try for a moment’s peace, and then I stumble on you fellows!—At least—I beg your pardon—I don’t quite mean that, you know.”
There was a rustle behind them, from a hedge where last year’s leaves still clung thick, and a striped head with high shoulders behind it peered out at them.
“Come on, old Badger!” shouted the Rat.
The Badger walked a pace or two toward them; then he grunted, “H’m! Company,” turned his back, and vanished.
“That’s _just_ the kind of fellow he is!” said the disappointed Rat. “Can’t stand Society! Well, that’s the last we’ll see of him today. Now, tell us, _who’s_ out on the river?”
“For one, Toad’s out on the water,” the Otter answered. “Racing boat brand-new, clothes brand-new, everything brand-new!”
The two animals looked at each other and laughed.

“First it was nothing but sailing,” said the Rat. “Then he got tired of that and took up punting. Nothing would do but he must punt all day, every day, and he made a fine mess of it. Last year it was living on a houseboat, and all of us had to go and stay with him on it and pretend we liked it. He was going to spend the rest of his life on a houseboat. It’s always the same, whatever he takes up: he gets tired of it and starts on something new.”
“A thoroughly decent fellow, though,” the Otter remarked thoughtfully. “But he’s no good at keeping steady—least of all in a boat!”

From where they sat they could catch a glimpse of the main stream across the island that lay between them, and just then a racing boat flashed into view. The rower—a short, stout figure—was splashing badly and rolling about a great deal, but working as hard as he could. The Rat stood up and called to him, but Toad—for it was he—only shook his head and settled grimly back to his rowing.
“If he keeps lurching around like that, he’ll be out of that boat in a minute,” said the Rat, settling back down.
“He certainly will,” the Otter chuckled. “Have I ever told you that good story about Toad and the lock-keeper? Here’s how it went. Toad....”

A wandering May-fly swerved unsteadily across the current, in the tipsy way that young blades among May-flies have when they’re seeing life. There was a swirl of water and a “cloop!” and the May-fly was not to be seen anymore.
Neither was the Otter.
The Mole looked down. The voice was still ringing in his ears, but the grass where the Otter had sprawled was plainly empty. There was not an Otter to be seen, all the way to the distant horizon.
But then there was a streak of bubbles on the surface of the river again.
The Rat hummed a little tune, and Mole remembered that animal manners forbid any comment whatever when a friend vanishes suddenly, whether for some reason or for none at all.
“Well, well,” said the Rat, “I suppose we ought to be getting along. I wonder which of us had better pack the lunch basket?” He did not sound as if he was terribly keen on the job.
“Oh, please let me,” said the Mole. So, of course, the Rat let him.

Packing the basket was not nearly as pleasant as unpacking it. It never is. But the Mole was determined to enjoy everything. Just when he had packed the basket and strapped it up tight, he spotted a plate staring up at him from the grass. When that was fixed, the Rat pointed out a fork that anybody ought to have seen. And last of all, what do you know, there was the mustard pot, which he had been sitting on without realizing it. Still, somehow the job got finished at last, without much loss of temper.

The afternoon sun hung low as the Rat rowed gently homeward in a dreamy frame of mind, murmuring bits of poetry to himself and paying Mole little notice. But Mole was stuffed with lunch and brimming with satisfaction and pride, and he already felt perfectly at home in a boat (or so he believed). He was getting fidgety too, and before long he said, “Ratty! Please, _I_ want a turn at the oars now!”
The Rat shook his head, smiling. “Not yet, my young friend,” he said. “Wait until you’ve had a few lessons first. It’s not as easy as it looks.”

For a minute or two Mole kept quiet. But he grew more and more envious of the Rat, who rowed along so strongly and effortlessly, and his pride began whispering that he could do just as well. All at once he leaped to his feet and snatched the oars. The Rat, who was staring out over the water and reciting more poetry to himself, was so startled that he toppled backwards off his seat, heels in the air, for the second time that day. Mole, in triumph, took his place and gripped the oars, completely sure of himself.
“Stop that, you _silly_ ass!” the Rat shouted from the floor of the boat. “You can’t manage it! You’ll capsize us!”

Mole swung the oars back with a flourish and took an enormous stab at the water. He missed the surface completely, his legs shot up over his head, and he found himself sprawled on top of the Rat, who was lying flat. In a great fright he grabbed for the side of the boat, and in the next instant—Sploosh!
Over went the boat, and he found himself struggling in the river.

Oh my, how cold the water was, and oh, how _very_ wet it felt! How it sang in his ears as he sank down, down, down! How bright and welcoming the sun looked when he bobbed up to the surface, coughing and sputtering! How black his despair was when he felt himself going under again! Then a strong paw clamped onto the scruff of his neck. It was the Rat, and plainly he was laughing. Mole could _feel_ him laughing, all the way down his arm and through his paw and into Mole’s own neck.

The Rat took hold of an oar and shoved it under one of Mole’s arms, then did the same on the other side. Then, swimming behind, he pushed the helpless animal ashore, hauled him out, and plunked him down on the bank, a soggy, sodden heap of misery.

Once the Rat had given him a rubdown and wrung out some of the water, he said, “Now then, old fellow! Run up and down the towpath as fast as you can until you’re warm and dry again, and I’ll go diving for the lunch basket.”

So the miserable Mole, wet on the outside and ashamed on the inside, trotted about until he was fairly dry. Meanwhile the Rat plunged into the water again, recovered the boat, set her right side up and tied her fast, fetched his floating belongings ashore a few at a time, and finally dived successfully for the lunch basket and struggled to land with it.

When everything was ready for another start, Mole, limp and downcast, sat down in the back of the boat. As they pushed off, he said in a low voice, shaky with feeling, “Ratty, my generous friend! I’m truly sorry for the foolish and ungrateful way I behaved. I feel quite faint when I think that I might have lost that beautiful lunch basket. I’ve been a complete donkey, and I know it. Will you forgive me this once, and let us carry on as we were?”

“Don’t give it another thought, bless you!” the Rat replied cheerfully. “What’s a little wet to a Water Rat? Most days I’m in the water more than I’m out of it. Don’t think about it anymore. And listen, I truly believe you should come and stay with me for a while. It’s very plain and rough, mind you—nothing like Toad’s house, though you haven’t seen that yet—but I can make you comfortable. I’ll teach you to row and to swim, and before long you’ll be as handy on the water as any of us.”

Mole was so moved by this kind way of talking that he couldn’t find his voice to answer, and had to wipe away a tear or two with the back of his paw. The Rat, kindly, looked off in another direction, and soon Mole’s spirits lifted again. He even managed to talk right back to a pair of moorhens who were snickering together about how bedraggled he looked.

Back at the house, the Rat built a cheerful fire in the parlor and settled Mole in an armchair in front of it, after fetching him a dressing gown and slippers. Then he told him river stories until suppertime. They were thrilling stories indeed to a creature who lived underground, like Mole. They were stories of weirs and sudden floods and leaping pike, and of steamers that hurled hard bottles (at any rate bottles were certainly hurled, and _from_ steamers, so presumably _by_ them). There were stories of herons, and how choosy they were about whom they spoke to; of adventures down drains, and night fishing with Otter, or long trips far afield with Badger. Supper was a very merry meal, but soon afterward his thoughtful host had to lead a dreadfully sleepy Mole upstairs to the best bedroom. There he laid his head on the pillow in great peace and happiness, knowing that his newfound friend the River was lapping at his windowsill.

This day was only the first of many like it for the liberated Mole, each one longer and fuller of interest as the ripening summer moved on. He learned to swim and to row, and he entered into the joy of running water; and with his ear to the reed stems he caught, now and then, something of what the wind was forever whispering among them.
